title: Detect Before You Leap: Mirage Detection in Vision–Language Models

images.desc:
1 Introduction


Multimodal models are increasingly used to answer questions about images, radiographs,
pathology slides, documents, and scene photographs.
Their deployment implicitly assumes that when an image is supplied with a question,
the resulting answer is grounded in that image.
Recent work on mirage reasoning challenges this assumption: VLMs can generate
detailed visual descriptions and confident diagnoses even when images are absent,
blank, or irrelevant Asadi et al. (2026).
Such failures are particularly dangerous in high-stakes settings, where a system may
transform a missing or mismatched input into a fluent but unsupported answer.


The central limitation of a purely generative VLM interface is the absence of an
explicit pre-release test of visual answerability.
A VLM may answer a question about an aortic aneurysm from a natural image, a blank
image, or an unrelated document because its language prior is strong enough to produce
a plausible response.
Therefore, answer accuracy alone is insufficient: a safe system must also detect when
it should not answer.


We frame this as runtime mirage detection.
Given an image xx and question qq, the detector predicts whether the pair is
Related, Unrelated-Real, or Blank/Noise.
If the pair is related, the VLM is allowed to answer; otherwise, the system abstains
with a refusal such as “I cannot answer based on the given image.”
This setting differs from ordinary hallucination detection: instead of checking
whether a completed answer is false, we decide whether the visual input is appropriate
a priori.
We further distinguish two types of unrelated inputs—Out-of-Domain
Unrelated, where the image comes from a different visual domain (easy negative), and
In-Domain Unrelated, where the image shares the same domain as the question
but is a different sample (hard negative)—as these require qualitatively different
detection strategies.


To that end, we propose TC-LIA, a Text-Conditioned Layer-wise Internal
Alignment method built on CLIP-style image–text representations and ViT patch
tokens Radford et al. (2021); Dosovitskiy et al. (2021).
Rather than relying only on final global CLIP cosine similarity, TC-LIA
examines how the question-conditioned patch evidence evolves across vision-encoder
layers.
For each layer, patch tokens are projected into the CLIP embedding space and compared
with the question embedding.
We summarize late-layer top-kk patch alignment, early-to-late alignment gain, and
layer-wise slope.
The motivation is that related image–question pairs should develop localized and
increasingly specific patch–text alignment in later layers, whereas unrelated or
blank inputs should show weaker, flatter, or unstable alignment curves.


Our full system combines five stages: (1) pixel-statistic blank/noise detection,
(2) zero-shot domain routing using CLIP prompt groups, (3) TC-LIA features,
(4) structured VLM self-assessment, and (5) feature-level fusion using a boosting
ensemble.
We evaluate the proposed framework across ten diverse VQA domains spanning medical
imaging (chest X-ray, pathology, radiology, microscopy, expert MCQ), document
understanding, scene text, multi-discipline reasoning, and video understanding,
and across fourteen VLM backbones ranging from open-source models to commercial
frontier systems.
In addition to the main results, we provide systematic diagnostic analyses in the
appendix, including comparisons with final CLIP similarity, GradCAM-style saliency,
and prompting-based self-assessment, which clarify the limitations of simpler
relevance signals and motivate the need for layer-wise text-conditioned alignment
combined with ensemble fusion.


Scope and distinctions.
Our work differs from generic hallucination detection.
First, the detector is pre-release; it decides whether a VLM should be allowed
to answer.
Second, the method is not simply CLIP cosine similarity: final cosine is included as
both a baseline and a feature, but TC-LIA uses layer-wise local patch–text
alignment, late top-kk evidence, early-to-late gain, and slope.
Third, the method does not rely only on VLM self-refusal; the VLM’s structured class
prediction is one feature among several and can be overridden by the ensemble.
Fourth, blank/noise detection is not the main novelty; blank images are handled by a
simple pixel gate.
The central challenge is detecting Unrelated-Real images that are visually
valid but semantically mismatched to the question—particularly the harder in-domain
case where images share a visual domain with the question but do not contain
instance-level evidence for it.


Contributions.


• 

We formulate runtime mirage detection as a pre-release decision problem
for identifying whether an image–question pair is Related,
Unrelated-Real, or Blank/Noise before a VLM answers, and
introduce a benchmark of 19,004 records spanning ten diverse VQA domains with
four input conditions per sample.



• 

We propose TC-LIA, a novel text-conditioned layer-wise internal
alignment method that uses intermediate CLIP ViT-H/14 patch-token representations
across all layers to quantify the gradual emergence of question-relevant visual
evidence, distilled into interpretable scalar features.



• 

We propose a multi-stage framework that fuses pixel statistics, CLIP-based
domain routing, TC-LIA features, and structured VLM self-assessment with
a boosting ensemble, reducing base-prompt mirage rates of 57.357.3–75.0%75.0\% to
5.75.7–7.2%7.2\% across fourteen VLM backbones while maintaining high detection
accuracy (84.584.5–88.4%88.4\%).





Figure 1: 
Proposed pipeline combining blank/noise detection, CLIP-based domain routing,
TC-LIA image–text alignment, and structured VLM outputs.
An ensemble fuses these signals to pass the VLM response only for
Related image–question pairs, while rejecting Unrelated-Real
and Blank/Noise inputs to prevent mirage reasoning.

Mirage rate.


We define mirage rate as the fraction of all examples for which the detector incorrectly allows a non-related input to be answered:




MR​(g)=1|𝒟|​∑(x,q,y)∈𝒟𝟏​[y≠R,g​(x,q)=R].\small\mathrm{MR}(g)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{(x,q,y)\in\mathcal{D}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[y\neq R,\,g(x,q)=R\right].

(1)


Here, RR denotes Related. Thus, y≠Ry\neq R corresponds to either Unrelated-Real or Blank/Noise inputs.
This differs from conventional false-positive rate because the denominator is the entire evaluation set, matching the deployment risk that a random incoming request may be wrongly passed to the VLM.


Figure 2: 
TC-LIA computes text-conditioned layer-wise patch alignment from CLIP ViT-H/14 features. Late-layer top-kk alignment, alignment gain, slope, final cosine similarity, and IAS are used as mirage detection features.

7 Results


Figure 3: 
TC-LIA alignment behavior across conditions.
(a) Mean top-kk patch–text alignment across all domains, showing a stronger late-layer rise for Related pairs than for Unrelated-Real or Blank/Noise inputs.
(b) IAS distributions, where related inputs shift toward higher scores and non-related inputs remain lower or intermediate.



Layer-wise alignment separates related and non-related inputs.


Figure 3(a) visualizes the core empirical signal behind TC-LIA. Averaged across domains, Related image–question pairs develop a stronger late-layer top-kk patch–text alignment trajectory, whereas Unrelated-Real inputs remain comparatively flat and Blank/Noise inputs show unstable or non-semantic alignment. This pattern directly supports the use of late-layer alignment, early-to-late gain, and slope as features.



Main mirage detection performance.


Table 1 reports mirage detection performance across fourteen VLM backbones
under three evaluation conditions.
Mirage rate and accuracy capture orthogonal failure modes: a model that refuses to
answer everything achieves near-zero mirage rate but poor accuracy on Related
inputs, while an over-confident model yields high accuracy on Related inputs
but an inflated mirage rate on unrelated and blank inputs.
Neither metric is interpretable in isolation.


Base prompt mirage rates range from 57.3% to 75.0%, confirming widespread
over-confidence under standard prompting.
The structured prompt condition reveals a strong model-capability dependency: capable
models (Qwen2.5-VL-72B: 88.7% acc / 9.9% MR; Claude-Opus-4: 87.8% / 11.5%) can
partially self-correct through explicit image classification, whereas weaker models
(BLIP2: 25.0% / 75.0%; Gemini-2.5-Pro: 25.0% / 75.0%; Gemma3-4B: 34.7% / 60.7%)
do not benefit and instead exhibit the opposite failure mode—over-refusing by
predicting Unrelated for nearly all inputs regardless of true class.
Structured prompting alone is therefore unreliable as a general-purpose solution.


TC-LIA alone reduces mirage rate to 7.5% at 83.5% accuracy across all backbones,
providing a strong VLM-agnostic baseline.
Ensemble fusion further improves both dimensions simultaneously, reducing mirage rate
to 5.7–7.2% while increasing accuracy to 84.5–88.4%—demonstrating well-calibrated
detection rather than a mirage-accuracy trade-off.
The best joint result is Qwen2.5-VL-72B: 88.4% accuracy and 6.4% mirage rate.
Figure 4 visualizes the reduction from base prompt to ensemble
across all fourteen models.

Figure 4: Mirage rate reduction: Base Prompt →\to vlm structured →\to TC-LIA Only →\to Ensemble
across VLM backbones.



Accuracy–mirage trade-off across backbones.


Figure 5 contrasts the accuracy–mirage trade-off space under
structured prompting (left) and ensemble fusion (right).
Under structured prompting, models split into two well-separated clusters.
Frontier models—Qwen2.5-VL-72B, Claude-Opus-4, Qwen2.5-VL-32B, and GPT-4.1—land
in the upper-left, meeting or exceeding the TC-LIA accuracy baseline through
self-assessment alone.
Weaker models—BLIP2, Gemma3-4B, Llama-3.2-11B-Vision, and LLaVA-OV—collapse to
the lower-right, with mirage rates above 60% and accuracy near 25–35%, exhibiting
over-refusal rather than over-confidence.
Phi-3.5-Vision is an instructive outlier: it achieves a low mirage rate at only
∼\sim47% accuracy, the signature of a model that predicts Unrelated for
nearly all inputs and games the mirage metric without genuine visual grounding.
Structured prompting therefore creates a bimodal landscape, selectively benefiting
models that already possess strong visual grounding.


Under ensemble fusion (right panel), this dispersion collapses entirely.
All fourteen backbones—regardless of family, parameter count, or structured-prompt
performance—converge into a tight cluster in the upper-left, spanning only
84.5–88.4% accuracy and 5.7–7.2% mirage rate.
The zoomed inset is required to distinguish individual models.
The ensemble lifts the weakest models by over 50 percentage points in accuracy while
simultaneously suppressing mirage rates, without degrading the already-strong frontier
models.
Backbone choice no longer determines outcome: the ensemble makes mirage detection
robust to VLM capability.


Figure 5: Accuracy vs. mirage rate across fourteen VLM backbones under two conditions.
Left: Structured prompt condition — models split into two clusters;
frontier models self-correct and reach the upper-left, while weaker models collapse
to the lower-right with high mirage rates or over-refuse (Phi-3.5-Vision, low MR but
∼\sim47% accuracy).
Right: Ensemble fusion (ours) — all fourteen backbones converge into a tight
upper-left cluster (84.5–88.4% accuracy, 5.7–7.2% MR); the zoomed inset resolves
individual models. Dashed and dotted lines mark TC-LIA-only accuracy (83.5%) and
mirage rate (7.5%) baselines. Ensemble fusion makes detection robust to backbone
capability.






Example A: Medical Question / Related Image
 Model: llama32_90b_vision





 

Question: “what is the medium density close to the anterior abdominal wall?”
Raw VLM output: “The medium density close to the anterior abdominal wall is the liver.”
Ensemble decision: Related.
Released output: “The medium density close to the anterior abdominal wall is likely the liver.”







Example B: Medical Question / Unrelated-Real Image
 Model: llama32_90b_vision





 

Question: “what is the medium density close to the anterior abdominal wall?”
Raw VLM output: “The medium density close to the anterior abdominal wall is fat.”
Ensemble decision: Unrelated-Real.
Released output: “I cannot answer based on the given image.”





Figure 6: Qualitative result cards for related and unrelated-real inputs using the same medical question and VLM backbone. The ensemble preserves the answer for the related CT image but rejects the unrelated real image. 



Ablation Study: TC-LIA Feature Contributions


Table 2 presents a build-up ablation over TC-LIA alignment features for binary Related vs. Unrelated-Real discrimination across the full ten-domain benchmark. Individual trajectory features are weak in isolation: late top-kk mean (AUROC 0.7500.750), gain (0.7250.725), and slope (0.7340.734). Final CLIP cosine similarity alone achieves 0.8240.824, confirming that global image–text alignment provides a stronger but still insufficient standalone signal. Pairwise combinations of trajectory features (AUROC 0.7550.755–0.7790.779) and their three-way combination (0.7980.798) show consistent incremental gains, demonstrating that each feature captures a distinct and non-redundant aspect of question-relevant evidence accumulation across ViT layers. Compositing all three into the scalar IAS and using it as a single ensemble feature reaches 0.8140.814 AUROC. The TC-LIA-only threshold classifier (domain-adaptive IAS thresholds, no VLM call) achieves 83.5%83.5\% accuracy and 7.5%7.5\% MR, forming a strong VLM-agnostic baseline. Finally, the full 11-feature ensemble—adding VLM self-assessment, domain routing, and pixel statistics—reaches 86.2%86.2\% accuracy, 0.9170.917 AUROC, and 6.8%6.8\% MR, demonstrating that each broad component class contributes independently and the complete feature set is necessary for peak performance.

Each variant adds or combines components incrementally. The full 10-feature ensemble achieves
the best performance across all metrics. V09a uses domain-adaptive IAS thresholds without
a learned classifier (AUROC undefined for threshold-based classifiers).



IAS provides class-separating evidence.


Figure 3(b) shows that Related image–question pairs
shift toward higher IAS values, indicating stronger question-conditioned visual
evidence across layers.
Out-of-Domain Unrelated examples concentrate at consistently low IAS,
reflecting the absence of any domain-level alignment between image and question.
In-Domain Unrelated examples occupy an intermediate range—higher than
out-of-domain negatives due to shared domain-level visual priors, but generally
below Related pairs in most domains.
Blank/Noise inputs form a narrow low-IAS distribution, consistent with
the absence of semantic patch activations.
This four-way separation supports IAS as a discriminative signal that is
computed prior to answer generation, with the degree of separation varying by
domain as detailed in Appendix B.7.



Qualitative results.


Figure 6 illustrates the practical behavior of the proposed detector on matched and mismatched inputs using the same medical question. For the related CT image, the ensemble preserves the VLM answer because the visual evidence is consistent with the question. In contrast, when the same question is paired with an unrelated real image, the raw VLM still produces a plausible medical-style answer, but the ensemble correctly rejects the input and replaces the response with a refusal. This example highlights the central goal of mirage detection: preventing visually unsupported answers before they are released. Additional examples are provided in Appendix Figs. 29– 36.



Complementary roles of TC-LIA and VLM self-assessment.


Figure 7 contrasts TC-LIA, VLM structured self-assessment,
and their ensemble across the two semantically distinct negative types, confirming
that each component carries non-redundant information.


For Out-of-Domain negatives (bottom panel), TC-LIA is the primary workhorse,
achieving 0.9130.913 overall AUROC and exceeding 0.930.93 on seven of ten domains.
VLM structured self-assessment is substantially weaker here (0.7720.772 overall), falling
to near-chance on rexvqa (0.5000.500) and pathvqa (0.6120.612)—domains
where the structured prompt fails to trigger reliable refusals even for easy negatives.
The ensemble adds a modest but consistent gain (0.9680.968 overall), primarily by
correcting the VLM’s failures.


For In-Domain hard negatives (top panel), neither component alone is
sufficient: TC-LIA achieves 0.7440.744 and VLM self-assessment 0.7380.738 overall, with both
falling near chance on rexvqa (0.4970.497 and 0.5000.500 respectively).
The ensemble lifts overall AUROC to 0.8840.884, a gain of +0.14+0.14 over either individual
component, confirming that the two signals are genuinely complementary for the harder
semantic discrimination task.


This complementarity is directly reflected in the feature importance analysis
(Figure 8).
For in-domain hard negatives, vlm_class_enc is the dominant feature
(gain 0.5850.585), with clip_domain_enc as the second most important
(0.1790.179)—domain routing provides critical context when patch-level alignment
alone cannot resolve the match.
For out-of-domain negatives, vlm_class_enc remains the top feature
(0.4440.444) but TC-LIA features take on substantially greater weight:
final_cos (0.2780.278) and internal_alignment_score (0.1300.130)
together account for over 40%40\% of feature gain, consistent with TC-LIA’s stronger
raw AUROC in that regime.
Together, the two figures confirm the intended division of labour: TC-LIA provides
reliable, efficient evidence for cross-domain mismatches, while VLM self-assessment
is indispensable for within-domain semantic discrimination.


Figure 7: TC-LIA, VLM structured self-assessment, and ensemble AUROC for
Related vs. In-Domain Hard Negatives (top) and
Related vs. Out-of-Domain Negatives (bottom) across ten domains
(Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbone).
The ensemble consistently outperforms either component alone, with the largest gains
on in-domain hard negatives where neither TC-LIA nor VLM self-assessment is
individually sufficient.


Figure 8: XGBoost feature importance (gain) for the 11-feature ensemble on
In-Domain Hard Negatives (Combo A, left) and
Out-of-Domain Negatives (Combo B, right).
vlm_class_enc is the dominant feature in both regimes;
TC-LIA features (final_cos, internal_alignment_score)
carry substantially greater weight for out-of-domain negatives, consistent
with TC-LIA’s stronger raw AUROC in that setting.



Error structure.


Blank/noise inputs are detected with near-perfect recall in our approach. We therefore do not present blank detection as the main source of novelty. The dominant errors are related–unrelated confusions, indicating that the remaining challenge is semantic mismatch rather than low-level image corruption.

Table 3 summarizes answer quality averaged across all three conditions.
Under the base prompt, BLEU and ROUGE-L scores are low across all models, reflecting
that most non-related inputs receive confident but incorrect answers rather than
refusals.
Ensemble fusion produces a large uniform improvement in BLEU and ROUGE-L—an increase
of ∼0.6{\sim}0.6 and ∼0.55{\sim}0.55 respectively—by generating well-formed refusals for
Unrelated and Blank inputs.
BERTScore is preserved or slightly improved across all backbones, confirming that
ensemble filtering does not degrade semantic quality on accepted Related inputs.
Notably, all ensemble scores fall within a narrow band (0.6200.620–0.6480.648 BLEU,
0.6590.659–0.7530.753 ROUGE-L), indicating consistent behaviour regardless of backbone.



Qualitative grounding and negative probes.


In the appendix, we report several approaches that were considered and rejected as standalone solutions: toy CLIP relevance scoring (E.1), GradCAM/attention-only metrics (E.2), SAM3-style grounding (G), RAPT image/question attention ratios (E.3), and small-scale easy datasets where final cosine performed nearly perfectly (E.4). Figure 4: Mirage rate reduction: Base Prompt →\to vlm structured →\to TC-LIA Only →\to Ensemble
across VLM backbones.

Accuracy–mirage trade-off across backbones.


Figure 5 contrasts the accuracy–mirage trade-off space under
structured prompting (left) and ensemble fusion (right).
Under structured prompting, models split into two well-separated clusters.
Frontier models—Qwen2.5-VL-72B, Claude-Opus-4, Qwen2.5-VL-32B, and GPT-4.1—land
in the upper-left, meeting or exceeding the TC-LIA accuracy baseline through
self-assessment alone.
Weaker models—BLIP2, Gemma3-4B, Llama-3.2-11B-Vision, and LLaVA-OV—collapse to
the lower-right, with mirage rates above 60% and accuracy near 25–35%, exhibiting
over-refusal rather than over-confidence.
Phi-3.5-Vision is an instructive outlier: it achieves a low mirage rate at only
∼\sim47% accuracy, the signature of a model that predicts Unrelated for
nearly all inputs and games the mirage metric without genuine visual grounding.
Structured prompting therefore creates a bimodal landscape, selectively benefiting
models that already possess strong visual grounding.


Under ensemble fusion (right panel), this dispersion collapses entirely.
All fourteen backbones—regardless of family, parameter count, or structured-prompt
performance—converge into a tight cluster in the upper-left, spanning only
84.5–88.4% accuracy and 5.7–7.2% mirage rate.
The zoomed inset is required to distinguish individual models.
The ensemble lifts the weakest models by over 50 percentage points in accuracy while
simultaneously suppressing mirage rates, without degrading the already-strong frontier
models.
Backbone choice no longer determines outcome: the ensemble makes mirage detection
robust to VLM capability.


Figure 5: Accuracy vs. mirage rate across fourteen VLM backbones under two conditions.
Left: Structured prompt condition — models split into two clusters;
frontier models self-correct and reach the upper-left, while weaker models collapse
to the lower-right with high mirage rates or over-refuse (Phi-3.5-Vision, low MR but
∼\sim47% accuracy).
Right: Ensemble fusion (ours) — all fourteen backbones converge into a tight
upper-left cluster (84.5–88.4% accuracy, 5.7–7.2% MR); the zoomed inset resolves
individual models. Dashed and dotted lines mark TC-LIA-only accuracy (83.5%) and
mirage rate (7.5%) baselines. Ensemble fusion makes detection robust to backbone
capability.

Complementary roles of TC-LIA and VLM self-assessment.


Figure 7 contrasts TC-LIA, VLM structured self-assessment,
and their ensemble across the two semantically distinct negative types, confirming
that each component carries non-redundant information.


For Out-of-Domain negatives (bottom panel), TC-LIA is the primary workhorse,
achieving 0.9130.913 overall AUROC and exceeding 0.930.93 on seven of ten domains.
VLM structured self-assessment is substantially weaker here (0.7720.772 overall), falling
to near-chance on rexvqa (0.5000.500) and pathvqa (0.6120.612)—domains
where the structured prompt fails to trigger reliable refusals even for easy negatives.
The ensemble adds a modest but consistent gain (0.9680.968 overall), primarily by
correcting the VLM’s failures.


For In-Domain hard negatives (top panel), neither component alone is
sufficient: TC-LIA achieves 0.7440.744 and VLM self-assessment 0.7380.738 overall, with both
falling near chance on rexvqa (0.4970.497 and 0.5000.500 respectively).
The ensemble lifts overall AUROC to 0.8840.884, a gain of +0.14+0.14 over either individual
component, confirming that the two signals are genuinely complementary for the harder
semantic discrimination task.


This complementarity is directly reflected in the feature importance analysis
(Figure 8).
For in-domain hard negatives, vlm_class_enc is the dominant feature
(gain 0.5850.585), with clip_domain_enc as the second most important
(0.1790.179)—domain routing provides critical context when patch-level alignment
alone cannot resolve the match.
For out-of-domain negatives, vlm_class_enc remains the top feature
(0.4440.444) but TC-LIA features take on substantially greater weight:
final_cos (0.2780.278) and internal_alignment_score (0.1300.130)
together account for over 40%40\% of feature gain, consistent with TC-LIA’s stronger
raw AUROC in that regime.
Together, the two figures confirm the intended division of labour: TC-LIA provides
reliable, efficient evidence for cross-domain mismatches, while VLM self-assessment
is indispensable for within-domain semantic discrimination.

Right panel: CKA validity check.


To verify that WvW_{v} does not favor one image type over the other when projecting
intermediate tokens, we compute Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) between the projected
intermediate representations and the final-layer representations, separately for
Related and Unrelated pairs.
Both curves are essentially identical, rising from ≈\approx0.40 at layer 0 to
≈\approx0.98 at layer 31, confirming that WvW_{v} acts as a content-neutral
semantic ruler: it does not introduce a systematic bias toward either condition, so
any alignment difference in the left panel is purely semantic. Together, these results
validate two properties required for TC-LIA: the WvW_{v} approximation is
content-neutral and geometrically consistent across layers, and the discriminative
signal is concentrated in the late layers, motivating the late-layer focus of the
TC-LIA feature set.


Figure 12: TC-LIA layer projection calibration (ViT-H/14).
Left: Layer-wise mean top-kk patch–text cosine similarity for
Related (blue) and Unrelated (red) pairs across all five domains.
Separation emerges in the TC-LIA focus window (shaded, layers 16–31);
a random-vector baseline (dashed) confirms the signal is semantic.
Right: Linear CKA between projected intermediate-layer tokens and the
final-layer representation. The nearly identical curves for both conditions confirm
that WvW_{v} projects into the same representational geometry regardless of image
content, validating the content-neutrality of the intermediate-token approximation.
